Proscribe

proh-SKRYBE · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To proscribe is to forbid, denounce, or condemn, especially by authority.

The league's new bylaws proscribe any form of betting among players.

Worked Example

Ancient Roman law could proscribe a citizen entirely, stripping away property and protection at once.

This wasn't a mild suggestion -- it was an official, forceful condemnation backed by the full power of the law, which is exactly proscribe.

How Proscribe Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

forbid

forbid: refuse to allow something

outlaw

outlaw: make something illegal

Antonyms

endorse

endorse: officially approve of or support something

How Strong Is It? — discourage → proscribe → outlaw

discourage vs. proscribe

discourage vs. proscribe: Discouraging something just makes it less appealing; proscribing it makes it formally forbidden.

outlaw vs. proscribe

outlaw vs. proscribe: Proscribe can describe any formal condemnation, spoken or written; outlaw specifically means making something illegal under the law.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — pro-

prefix — pro-: before, publicly (Latin)

root — scrib

root — scrib: to write (Latin (scribere))

suffix — -e

suffix — -e: verb-forming ending (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Proscribe comes from Latin pro- ('before, publicly') + scribere ('to write') -- literally 'to write publicly,' recalling the ancient Roman practice of posting a condemned person's name where all could see it.

Use the root in a new word: describe

Use the root in a new word: describe: The same scribere root gives us describe (de- 'down' + scribere, 'to write down the details of') and inscribe.

Root Check

Word Choice

Proscribe is easy to confuse with its near-opposite-sounding cousin "prescribe" (to formally recommend or require) -- proscribe always means to forbid, never to recommend.
